newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ukrainian president sets Paris balancing test.
newsitem.headline: Ukrainian president sets Paris balancing test.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma visits France on Thursday at a time when Paris is seeking to balance its enthusiasm for Moscow with closer trade and political ties to the former Soviet republic.

Kuchma, whose country considers Paris a lukewarm partner among rich nations for aid and political backing, will meet President Jacques Chirac, Foreign Minister Herve de Charette and former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing on Thursday.
On Friday, the second and last day of his first official visit to France, Kuchma will address business leaders.
French Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said Ukraine, whose own ties with Russia have been overshadowed by disputes over the Black Sea fleet, had an important strategic position in Europe.

"This visit will be the chance to welcome the Ukrainian president's determination to reform, to encourage him on the route he has chosen and reaffirm our desire for the development of a strong and stable Ukraine, fully integrated into the international community," he told reporters.

Chirac, due to visit Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Sunday near Moscow where Yeltsin is recovering from pneumonia, is seeking to improve ties with Ukraine without upsetting strong French links to Russia.

"France and Ukraine have not developed relations very far since the Cold War," said Dominique Moisi, deputy director of the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI). "This is a way of recognising its independence.
"Relations with Russia can be developed independently. I believe Paris can be good friends with both Moscow and Kiev," he told Reuters.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Doutriaux said French investments in Ukraine doubled in 1996 from 1995 to 200 million francs ($40 million) and called it "an encouraging sign for the future".

As a symptom of Kiev's uncertainty about the strength of French commitment, some Ukraine diplomats say France is blocking Western aid to close the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, site of the world's worst nuclear disaster in 1986.

But Moisi said "the French are as conscious as others in the West of the dangers of nuclear leaks. The Ukrainians want as much cash as possible and I don't think one should see it as anything more than a commercial negotiation".

The Group of Seven leading industrialised states have pledged $3.1 billion in grants and credits to help Ukraine meet its pledge to close Chernobyl's one working reactor by 2000. Kiev complains that almost no cash has reached it yet.

Doutriaux said the two countries would also discuss closer security ties with the goal of "ensuring that each European state feels secure. In this perspective, we favour developing relations between NATO and Ukraine."
Ukraine, which tranferred the last of 1,800 Soviet nuclear warheads to Russia for dismantling in July, has no plans to seek NATO membership for the moment.
Worried that neighbouring states might join NATO and become the site of nuclear weapons, Kiev wants a nuclear weapons-free zone in Central and Eastern Europe.
